# SK1061 — Use `nameof`

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A name produced at run time — `typeof(T).Name`, an enum member's `ToString()` — or written as a literal in a position that is defined to hold an identifier.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | 6.0 |
| Since | 1.3 |
| ReSharper | `UseNameOfInsteadOfToString` (`resharper_use_name_of_instead_of_to_string_highlighting`) |

## Why

`nameof` is the only spelling of a name that a rename touches. `typeof(Widget).Name` and `Colour.Red.ToString()` compute at run time what the compiler already knows, and a literal `"count"` handed to `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`'s `paramName` is a name the compiler was never asked about at all — so it survives the rename that makes it wrong, and the first person to see the mistake is whoever reads the exception. This is disproportionately a generated-code problem: a model writes the string because the pre-C# 6 dialect it learned had nothing else to write.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException("count", count, null);
var name = typeof(Widget).Name;
var label = Colour.Red.ToString();
```

Write:

```csharp
throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(count), count, null);
var name = nameof(Widget);
var label = nameof(Colour.Red);
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **A string that happens to equal a member name is not a `nameof` candidate, and this rule never guesses.** Serialization keys, JSON property names, SQL column names, HTTP headers and `.editorconfig` keys are all literals that look exactly like identifiers and mean something a rename must *not* follow — rewriting one silently changes the wire format. There is no test that separates them from the intended ones, so the rule fires only in positions whose meaning is defined: a `paramName` parameter of the `ArgumentException` family, and a `PropertyChangedEventArgs`/`PropertyChangingEventArgs` constructor. ⚠ **`UseNameofExpressionForPartOfTheString` is deliberately not covered** for that reason; it is also the one of the three inspections that ships at `none`. ⚠ **`typeof(T).Name` is `nameof(T)` only for a non-generic named type spelled by its own name.** `typeof(List<int>).Name` is `` `List`1` `` and `nameof(List<int>)` is `List`; `typeof(int).Name` is `Int32` and `nameof(int)` does not compile; `typeof(T).Name` on a type parameter is the *argument's* name at run time; and a `using` alias makes `nameof` produce the alias where `Name` produces the type — so the last identifier of the written type must equal the symbol's own name. Arrays, nullable spellings and `dynamic` are all refused. ⚠ **An enum member's `ToString()` is its name only when the value is unique.** `enum E { A = 1, B = 1 }` makes `E.B.ToString()` return `"A"`, so the rule reads every field of the enum and declines a shared value. ⚠ `SK2017` reports the `paramName` literal that names *no* parameter and this rule reports the one that does, so the two never both fire. Every shape is silent inside an expression tree and below C# 6, and the four shapes share that one floor, so the gate is per-rule.
